new_statements.translation: [p.125] The most frequent 'koppelingen' (copulative compounds) are those in which two plural nouns become one whole; the stress always lies on the second member. [...] [p.129] Another example is hozenvouten, still heard in the Westerkwartier = 'stocking-feet', but with the stress at the end: Hai luip op hozenvouten. Everywhere else this word has been replaced by ... hozevórrels. This is not a 'koppeling' but an ordinary compound with the stress on the first member. [p.38-39] The adjective forms a compound with its noun when a single concept is expressed. Then the stress lies on the first member: n doodlid; de nijboer ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: No accessible description states a general word-stress rule for simplex words; the sources presuppose Dutch/Germanic stress and mark only deviations. What is stated first-hand: ordinary (determinative) compounds carry main stress on the first member; the characteristically Gronings copulative 'koppelingen' (aartenbonen, koppenoren, spekkenaaier, jongkat) carry it on the second member; the suffix -achteg is stressed when it means 'having' (dailachteg, woonachteg) but unstressed in geelachteg etc; Romance loans keep non-initial stress (muzikant, foabrikant, p.168). Reker 2002:50 adds that onverstandeg has 'net als in het Nederlands' main stress on the penult, shifting to the first syllable in the clipped noun onverstand.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing systematic; Reker 2002:36 mentions a 'bijklemtoon' on -um in trisyllabic place names (Middelstum > Middelsom) following the Groene Boekje rule; de Vries 1895 §9 notes a 'bijaccent' on the second element of falling diphthongs and §23 shortening before a syllable 'met den bijtoon'.
new_statements.exceptions: Copulative koppelingen with final-member stress (aartenbonen, hozenvouten, koppenoren, jongkat vs. jonkgoud); -achteg 'having' stressed; reusachteg stressed on the suffix although semantically in the other group (p.143); place-name compounds like 't Hooghoes, Graauwdiek 'dan ligt de klem achter, behalve in Nijstad' (p.39).
new_statements.domain_note: All statements concern morphologically complex words (compounds, derivations, loans) in citation form; the location of stress in monomorphemic native words is nowhere stated in the accessible sources (implicitly as in Dutch: ter Laan 1953:6 'De Groninger klinkers komen over 't algemeen met de Hollandse overeen'; Reker 2002:50 'net als in het Nederlands').
new_statements.identity_note: ter Laan 1953 and Reker 2002 describe Gronings as a whole (ter Laan's base is the Slochteren/southern Fivelgo variety, with Westerkwartier, Hogeland, Oldambt, Stad and Westerwolde variants flagged); de Vries 1895 is the Noordhorn (Westerkwartier) dialect; Schuringa 1923 centres on the Veenkoloniaals; Veldman 1992 is Westerwolds — all sub-dialects of Gronings (gron1242).

sources.citation: Vries, Wobbe de (1895). Het vocalisme van den tongval van Noordhorn. Proefschrift Rijksuniversiteit Groningen. Groningen: J.B. Wolters. 104 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Vowel study of the Noordhorn (Westerkwartier) dialect. Treats 'toonlooze' (unstressed) syllables (§7, §22-24: unstressed syllables are short, a following unstressed syllable shortens the stressed vowel), falling diphthongs with a 'bijaccent' (§9), and compound-like phrases 'met één hoofdaccent' (§78 Opm. 2); presupposes Germanic stress but states no placement rule.

sources.note: Ch. 2 'De klanken en hun spelling' is essayistic; no general stress rule. p.36-37: place names Winsum/Warffum have the hoofdklemtoon directly before -um, Middelstum has it on the first syllable with a bijklemtoon effect on -um; p.49-50: aalbegeer, antam, baloor, onverstand etc. 'alle met de nadruk op de eerste lettergreep'; 'Onverstandeg met net als in het Nederlands het belangrijkste accent op de voorlaatste lettergreep, wordt ingekort tot onverstand, en het accent verspringt naar de eerste lettergreep.'
